 Quick bites: A comeback is a start; consistency is the test for the Sharks
 Posted on October 30, 2026 October 30, 2026 by Annie Moore 
 For 40 minutes, the San Jose Sharks looked like a team waiting for something to happen. Then, within 2 minutes and 50 seconds, the Sharks made it happen themselves. The team’s 3-2 win over Vancouver on Thursday revealed a question far more important than how it escaped with two points: Can this group take control of a game before it has to rescue itself?
 The Sharks are learning to play with confidence without abandoning their structure. When things aren’t going the players’ way, they overthink. Plays get forced. They turn the puck over instead of trusting teammates with simple decisions.
 Following a slow start against the Vancouver Canucks on Thursday, San Jose overcame a two-goal deficit. This comeback highlights the team’s ability to generate offense when the players play faster and trust each other, but it also exposed their biggest weakness: under pressure, the Sharks tighten up, force plays and turn the puck over. The question remains whether they can turn that kind of third-period effort into a consistent 60-minute identity.
 “You could see it, could feel it,” Head Coach Ryan Warsofsky said. “So I give the group a lot of credit. The players went out there and just executed a fast, loose period. Got some energy, played smart, put pucks behind them, and we had success from that.”
 The Sharks are at a point in the team’s rebuild where winning is about establishing habits that will make them competitive long-term. A team that relies on third-period comebacks, individual brilliance and opponents making mistakes isn’t building sustainable success. For a young roster expected to grow together, learning to manage pressure, trust teammates, and generate consistent five-on-five offense is essential to becoming a team that can compete night after night. The Vancouver win showed both what the Sharks can do and what they still haven’t figured out.
 The San Jose Sharks erased a 2-0 deficit against Vancouver at the SAP Center, scoring three goals in the third period to win 3-2. Will Smith scored twice before Mason Marchment netted the go-ahead goal just 11 seconds after Smith’s equalizer. The comeback followed two periods of forced plays, turnovers and difficulty generating offense. 
 Warsofsky said his message was to “loosen up a little bit,” emphasizing the need to play faster, simplify decisions and trust one another. The bigger challenge is making that approach sustainable over a full 60 minutes rather than relying on late-game comebacks.
 “We’ve been frustrated with where our game’s at, and I think there’s a lot of potential for our group,” Warsofsky said. “But we have to play a certain way. So proud of the group to come back in the third … They did a hell of a job in the third period. We’re trying here.”
 The comeback against Vancouver offered a glimpse of what the Sharks can look like when they stop pressing and trust their structure. After two periods of forcing plays and struggling to generate offense, San Jose simplified its game in the third. They played faster, got pucks behind the Canucks and created momentum through sustained pressure. Warsofsky said the team had been “gripping it really tight,” adding that the message between periods was to “just go play, loosen up a little bit.”
 The Sharks showed they can adjust when frustration starts dictating their decisions. Now the question is whether they can recognize that moment earlier. The third period showed the adjustment can work; consistency will determine whether it becomes part of their identity.
 A young team cannot build a sustainable identity around needing a comeback to find its game. The Sharks are still learning how to respond when their offense stalls. Opponents take control, or mistakes pile up. 
 Their ability to simplify, support one another and create chances without forcing plays will be just as important as their scoring talent. Against Vancouver, they proved they could make that adjustment over one period. The next step is showing they can do it before falling behind and carry it consistently against tougher opponents.
 “We didn’t sit back,” Warsofsky said. “It’s not like we’ve sat on our heels. We are pushing up ice more, so that’s positive.”
